summary: Mandarin Chinese is the standard language of China and Taiwan and has more native speakers than any other language. Words never change their form; tones distinguish meanings; it is written in characters, and pinyin is the Latin spelling used for learning.

typology.why: No endings at all: 我吃, 他吃, 我们吃 — 吃 never changes. Time, number and questions are shown by separate words (了, 三个, 吗) and by word order.
typology.alsoShows: New words are mostly compounds of old ones: 电 ‘electric’ + 脑 ‘brain’ = 电脑 ‘computer’.

facts.label: Script
facts.value: Chinese characters — simplified (mainland China, Singapore) or traditional (Taiwan, Hong Kong); pinyin for pronunciation

facts.label: Where
facts.value: China, Taiwan, Singapore and Chinese communities worldwide

peculiarities.title: Tones
peculiarities.text: Every syllable has a tone: mā (high), má (rising), mǎ (low), mà (falling), ma (neutral). 妈 mā ‘mother’ and 马 mǎ ‘horse’ differ only in tone.

peculiarities.title: Measure words
peculiarities.text: Between a number (or 这/那) and a noun comes a measure word: 一个人, 三本书.

peculiarities.title: No tenses
peculiarities.text: Verbs do not change; time words (昨天) and particles (了, 过) say when and whether something happened.

peculiarities.title: Characters
peculiarities.text: Each character is a syllable with a meaning; you learn them through the words that contain them.

forYou.text: The basic word order is subject–verb–object, as in English: 我吃苹果 = I eat apples.
The opposite of Greek: no genders, no cases, no endings — but tones and measure words instead.

quiz.why: Words never change; grammar is word order and small separate words.

quiz.q: What tells 妈 mā ‘mother’ from 马 mǎ ‘horse’?
What comes between a number and a noun?
